Opening: The Never-Ending Royal Audience

Status: Strongly endorsed signature concept \| 22 November 2026

# Narrative setup

A king summons the playable band to the royal throne room. He earnestly launches into an incredibly important, elaborate briefing about an existential crisis, prophecy, ancient seals and the responsibilities of the chosen heroes. The world treats this as the opening of the greatest quest ever undertaken. The protagonists are distracted by everything in the room, asking about secret passages, the royal champion's remarkable armor, the advisor's talking dragon pet, curious potions and implausible contraptions.

# Foundational joke, operationalized

If the player politely does nothing, the king continues droning on almost indefinitely. He never reaches a normal “now go begin the game” handoff. The game begins when the player chooses to act. The first hidden puzzle is the realization that waiting for exposition is not necessary and never was. There is no forced quest acceptance, scripted skip prompt or “press X to continue” that resolves the opening as ordinary exposition.

# The three-hour alternative ending

If the player actually allows the speech to continue for approximately THREE HOURS, it finally becomes an unexpected end-credits sequence. The king's words flow seamlessly into acknowledging contributors, which becomes the actual credits roll. A real alternate ending is awarded without having left the throne room. This is meant to be unusually committed and discoverable, not announced up front. The precise runtime, credit implementation, save/replay state and post-credits behavior remain design questions. The ~3-hour commitment itself is user-proposed and enthusiastically endorsed.

# The royal court as a dense real level

The king: occupies a throne against a stained-glass window; players wonder if they can suplex him through it.

The champion: intimidating figure with magnificent powerful armor; players want to fight him, test the armor, or steal it.

The wizard/advisor: pockets, spellbook, mysterious pills and other valuable magical objects; players can pickpocket and experiment.

The captive dragon beast: legendary creature that once devastated the kingdom, held in a cage or magical restraint; players may try to release it, feed it stolen magical pills, befriend, flee or attack it.

Secret architecture: suspicious wall seams, passage behind throne, mechanical chandeliers, crawlspaces, locked doors, hidden treasury, royal transport or catwalks.

These props and placements are concrete examples of intended interactions, not final architectural blueprints. The captive beast and talking dragon pet might be the same creature or different ones; this is UNRESOLVED.

# Player agency from minute one

Allow movement, character switching, inspection, stealth, theft, attack and object manipulation during the speech. The player can listen, walk around, steal the crown, pickpocket the wizard, challenge the champion, explore a suspicious passage, release the dragon, consume or administer pills, assault the king, flee the hall or pursue an early quest lead. Do not impose an invisible “no combat during exposition” rule.

The palace should react convincingly. If the king is attacked, guards intervene; if the dragon breaks free, the court panics; if a valuable object is stolen unnoticed, the consequences may only emerge later.

# Character personality without taking control away

Thought bubbles, glances, body language and contextual remarks might signal different things each character finds epic. A grappler imagines the king flying through the window; a thief studies the wizard's pockets; a creature enthusiast wants the dragon; an explorer studies an uneven wall. Show a sampling, not glowing icons on every secret. The player should notice additional possibilities unaided.

# A speech with genuine endurance

The monologue should be original, continuously progressing, solemn in delivery, and increasingly digressive. It may move from the ancient apocalypse to royal genealogies, forgotten accords, inheritances, farming, etiquette and back to the sacred seals. Avoid an obvious short looping audio sample. Courtiers and guards may tire, change shifts or create fresh opportunities as time passes; the king remains committed. The opening must be skippable THROUGH PLAYER ACTION, not through a conventional exposition-skip mechanism.

# Multiple valid starting outcomes

Polite hero: listen for a while, accept an optional quest lead, exit to the world.

Curious explorer: locate passage, enter vault or cellar, begin a secret route.

Quiet thief: steal pills or keys, leave without alert.

Public menace: suplex king through stained glass; court escalates into an absurd pursuit.

Naturalist/trickster: release beast, improvise with pills, trigger a major catastrophe.

Patient contrarian: remain listening for about three hours and see secret credits.

No particular outcome is canonical. The game should not reset everybody to the same cutscene after the first disruption.

# Returning later

The throne room remains a valid explorable area in the overworld. New characters and powers allow previously impossible intrusions, battles, hidden passages and alternate routes. The king may be still seeking an occasion to finish his original message, but exact persistence and dialogue state are open.

# Vision-level acceptance test

A new player should discover at least three compelling distractions within 30 seconds of gaining control. The player should be able to interrupt the speech via at least one nonviolent and one outrageous action. The reaction should yield gameplay rather than a static “game over” or reload. A patient player should reach the special credits through actual passive waiting. The main quest should remain available without monopolizing their freedom.
